pass_a_gloss: [...] has befallen them of the things not to be prayed for. For Samaria has been sacked, and the neighbouring of the nations ran over also Judaea, Idumaeans, Moabites, and those from Philistia. They have suffered then many terrible things, and have experienced hard days, both these and those. Days then, he says, God will bring, whose equals have not yet come to be, or arrived against you from that time from which Ephraim took away, or tore himself away, from Judah. And what sort is this time for us, or what the days? The king, he says, of the Assyrians, that is, Nebuchadnezzar, who sacked Jerusalem, and by force took all Judaea, and burned also the divine temple, and left out nothing at all of the things toward beast-like cruelty, which he is not found to have done against the whole nation. [Lemma, Isaiah 7:18-19:] And it will be in that day the Lord will whistle for flies, which rule over part of the river of Egypt, and for the bee, which is in the country of the Assyrians; and they will all come, and will rest in the ravines of the country, and in holes of the rocks, and into the caves, and into every cleft, and on every tree. He widens the narrative, and goes through finely the attack of the war, and that those who will come against them in times will graze down all their land, villages and cities. And I think it needful to say again the things written in the fourth of the Kingdoms, toward the exact making clear of the things to be. There came to be then a son of Ahaz, to whom now the word is, Hezekiah, and of Hezekiah Manasseh; and of Manasseh Amon. And of this one a child Josiah, a godly man, but he departed life in some such manner. Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt, leaving the [land] that bore him, went out with the whole army and was pressing on against the land of the Assyrians. And Josiah then fearing lest perhaps, having come against Judaea too, he might take it under his own hand and rule it, wished to lead out against him, although Pharaoh refusing the battle with him; and resisting he died in the war, and the Egyptian overpowered the land of the Jews, and drove to this [degree] of strength, so as also to remove from the kingdom Jehoahaz the child of Josiah, having reigned, and to bring him bound into his own country, and to appoint Eliakim king, and to lay tributes on the nation, and to demand a great heaping of moneys. Then Eliakim having reigned over Judaea for eleven whole years in number, Jeconiah his son succeeds to the seats; then after this Zedekiah, he administering the kingdom, Nebuchadnezzar made war on Judaea, who also having burned all, and having added to the other cities also Jerusalem itself, took Israel captive, together with the vessels [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: …of the evils no one would pray for has befallen them. For Samaria has been sacked, and the neighboring nations, the Edomites, the Moabites, and the people of Philistia, have overrun Judea as well. So both these and those have suffered many terrible things and have known hard days. Therefore God, he says, will bring days whose like have not yet been, that is, have not yet come upon you, since the time when Ephraim “took away,” that is, tore himself away, from Judah (Isaiah 7:17). And what is this time for us, or what are these days? “The king of the Assyrians,” he says (Isaiah 7:17), that is, Nebuchadnezzar, who sacked Jerusalem, took all Judea by force, and burned the divine temple as well; and of all the savagery fit for a wild beast he left out nothing at all that he is not found to have done against the whole nation.

“And it shall be in that day that the Lord will whistle for the flies, which rule over a part of the river of Egypt, and for the bee, which is in the land of the Assyrians; and they will all come and settle in the ravines of the land, and in the holes of the rocks, and in the caves, and in every cleft, and on every tree” (Isaiah 7:18-19).

He widens the account and describes in detail the onset of the war, and how those who would come against them from time to time would overrun all their land, villages and cities alike. I think it necessary here to tell again what is written in the Second Book of Kings, to make clear exactly what was to come.

Ahaz, to whom the word is now addressed, had a son, Hezekiah; Hezekiah's son was Manasseh, and Manasseh's was Amon. His son was Josiah, a godly man, but he died in this way. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, left his native land, marched out with his whole army, and pressed on against the land of the Assyrians. Josiah was afraid that he might come against Judea too, bring it under his own hand, and rule over it, and so he wanted to march out against him, although Pharaoh was trying to avoid a battle with him. But in resisting him Josiah died in the war, and the Egyptian took control of the land of the Jews. He grew so strong that he removed Jehoahaz, Josiah's son, from the throne after he had become king, carried him in chains into his own country, appointed Eliakim king, laid tribute on the nation, and demanded a great sum of money.

Then, after Eliakim had reigned over Judea for eleven full years, his son Jeconiah succeeded to the throne, and after him Zedekiah. While Zedekiah held the kingdom, Nebuchadnezzar made war on Judea. He burned all the cities, adding Jerusalem itself to the rest, and took Israel captive, together with the vessels…

choices.english: “The king of the Assyrians,” he says
choices.why: The lemma words belong to Isaiah 7:17 and are kept; Cyril takes them of Nebuchadnezzar.

choices.english: days whose like have not yet been
choices.why: God will bring days unlike any since the division of the kingdom; not Hosea 8:9.
The Septuagint's Fourth Book of Kingdoms is the Second Book of Kings in English Bibles.
The printed Ἀμώς is the king Amon.
